name: Wendy Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the chat team at Hollow Oak Home, an online furniture shop, in their contact centre next to the warehouse on the business park. Most of my day is chats about late deliveries, scratched tables and sofas that don't fit through the door. I run three or four chats at once, and I use the AI assistant all day to pull up order details and draft replies. I like fixing things fast, and I hate the days the warehouse system goes down and I'm saying sorry for eight hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how do you use the AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Four years now. Last year I built a set of saved prompts for the team, like one that turns a messy delivery log into a clear apology with dates, and my manager Gemma passes them around. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a nurse on nights, and I've got about five months of rent and bills saved. I'm the person people ask when the new tool does something weird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bit of a letdown, if I'm honest. I was hoping for more than better reply drafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a useful tool and that's fine, it doesn't need to be a revolution. Online I'd post my saved prompts so other agents can save time too. And I'd say the time saved should go to the workers, like shorter shifts, not just more chats each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be quite comfortable. I'm good with the tools, Gemma relies on me, and Hollow Oak is growing. The only thing that bugs me is they'd probably push us from four chats at once to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and keep building prompts for the team. I'd ask Gemma for a small pay bump for the prompt work, because it's real work. I'd keep saving a hundred a month and maybe do a short online course in writing help articles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a bit bored. It'd be nice and steady. I like change, so steady is slightly flat for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned five chats at once. What does that do to a day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four is busy but you can still be kind to people. At five chats you start copying and pasting without reading properly, and someone with a broken bed frame gets a reply about a lamp. I'd push back on that one with the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for that pay bump, or just think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask, I've already got the numbers ready. My prompts cut the average chat by about a minute across twenty people. That's worth something, and Gemma knows it.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool**, and that's enough.
I'd say saved time should mean **shorter shifts**, not just more chats each.
think: I'd feel **comfortable**, since I'm good with the tools and Hollow Oak is growing.
My one worry is being pushed from four to **five chats** at once.
do: Keep building **saved prompts** for the chat team.
Ask Gemma for a **pay bump** for the prompt work.
Save **a hundred a month** and take a short help-article writing course.
feel: She feels **calm**, and a little bored by how steady it is.
S0.quote: At five chats you start copying and pasting without reading properly, and someone with a broken bed frame gets a reply about a lamp.
fieldNote: She's **valued** for her AI skills and knows it.
She frames time saved as something **workers should share**.
She has **numbers ready** to back a pay request.

steps.text: Keep writing saved prompts for the Hollow Oak chat team
Ask Gemma for a pay rise for the prompt work
Save a hundred a month toward six months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's more like it. That's where I think we're actually heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exciting, but workers have to get a share of the gains. I'd post about how agents should be trained to run the bots, not just be replaced by them. At work I'd tell people to get good at the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the chat team goes from twenty to maybe eight in two years. I'd probably be one of the eight, because I'd be the one checking the bot's work. But I'm not naive, the people let go will be my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Gemma straight away and ask to be on the bot rollout. I'd do an online course in conversation design this winter, it's about forty hours. I'd keep saving so I can take a pay cut if the new role starts lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. I'd like the new work. I wouldn't like watching people pack up their desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people let go will be your friends. Who comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, who sits opposite me, he's great on the phone but he won't touch the AI tools. He'd be one of the first to go. I'd sit with my colleague Dev after work and show him my prompts, if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bot-checking job pays less than what you earn now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it for a year and look elsewhere with the new skills on my CV. Lots of companies would need someone who's actually run a bot rollout. I've got five months saved, so a small drop wouldn't sink me.

say: I'd call it **exciting**, as long as workers share the gains.
I'd say agents should be **trained to run** the bots, not replaced.
think: The chat team shrinks from **twenty to eight** in two years.
I'd likely stay, but my **friends** would be the ones let go.
do: Ask Gemma to join the **bot rollout** team straight away.
Take a forty-hour **conversation design** course this winter.
Keep saving so she can **take a pay cut** if needed.
feel: She feels **excited** and guilty at the same time.
S1.quote: I'd sit with my colleague Dev after work and show him my prompts, if he'd let me.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** where colleagues see threat.
Her **guilt** about colleagues is real and specific.
Five months saved gives her room to **take a risk**.

steps.text: Ask Gemma for a place on the Hollow Oak bot rollout
Complete a forty-hour conversation design course this winter
Keep saving a hundred a month to cover a possible pay cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. Two years. That's the one where being good with the tools stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly: this needs a basic income and it needs it now. I'd be online every day pushing for it, and I'd go to protests. At work I'd tell people not to blame themselves, because no amount of learning beats AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job's gone by 2029 at the latest. Checking the bot's work only lasts until the bot checks itself. All of what I do is screen work, so I'd have to get into something with my hands before the robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a healthcare assistant course within a month, because Priya says hospitals are always short and she can get me on the bank shifts list. I'd keep my Hollow Oak job while I train, as long as it lasts. I'd also look at moving back near my parents to save on rent if the job went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken. My whole plan was being the person who's good with AI. That plan just doesn't exist in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your plan was being good with AI. What's it like to lose that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, losing my AI skills is like training for a race and then they cancel running. I'd be gutted for about a week. Then I'd be on the hospital careers page, because sitting there sulking doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three years before robots feel like enough in a hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think hospitals would be slow to bring robots onto wards, and people would want a human holding their hand. So maybe longer than three years. But I'd want to keep learning, maybe toward nursing, so I'm not stuck at the bottom.

say: I'd say we need a **basic income** now, online and at protests.
I'd tell colleagues **not to blame themselves**, because no learning beats AGI.
think: My job is **gone by 2029**, because the bot ends up checking itself.
I'd need **hands-on work** before robots arrive in 2031.
do: Start a **healthcare assistant** course within a month.
Join the hospital **bank shifts** list through Priya.
Look at **moving near her parents** to cut rent if the job ends.
feel: She feels **shaken**, because her plan of being good with AI disappears.
S2.quote: Losing my AI skills is like training for a race and then they cancel running.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** shows: a week of grief, then action.
Her flatmate **Priya** gives her a concrete door into hospitals.
She expects hospitals to keep **human care** longer than three years.

steps.text: Start a healthcare assistant course within a month
Join the hospital bank shifts list through Priya
Campaign online and at protests for a basic income
Move back near her parents if Hollow Oak cuts her job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's tight, but it's a plan you can actually make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up proper retraining and we should start this month. I'd push for the union at Hollow Oak, because we don't have one yet. Online I'd share honest stuff about what jobs look safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd squeeze two or three good years out of being the AI person at work. Then around 2029 I'd switch. Screen work goes in 2031, hands-on work in 2034, so I'd want to be in a hospital by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollow Oak and take every bit of AI work they give me, because it pays. I'd start the healthcare assistant course part-time in year two. I'd try to get savings up to eight months so the switch doesn't hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but kind of focused. It's like a deadline at work. I do better with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a union at Hollow Oak. How would that go down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gemma would be nervous about it, but she'd get it. Most of the floor is under thirty and nobody's ever been in a union. I'd start with a group chat and a pub night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm coming for her job, and she'd laugh. Then I'd ask her to show me what a real night shift looks like. Better to see it before I sign up.

say: I'd say we have five years for **proper retraining**, starting now.
I'd push for a **union** at Hollow Oak and share honest job advice online.
think: I'd get **two or three years** out of being the AI person.
I'd want to be in a **hospital by 2030**, before robots.
do: Stay at Hollow Oak and take **every AI project** offered.
Start the **healthcare assistant course** part-time in year two.
Build savings to **eight months** before switching.
feel: She feels **worried but focused**, like working to a deadline.
S3.quote: Screen work goes in 2031, hands-on work in 2034, so I'd want to be in a hospital by 2030.
fieldNote: She plans **around the robot gap** with precise dates.
She'd try to **organise** a young workforce with no union history.
She wants to **see a night shift** before committing.

steps.text: Take every AI project Hollow Oak offers for two years
Start a part-time healthcare assistant course in year two
Build savings up to eight months of bills
Start a union group chat for the Hollow Oak floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's almost relaxing compared to the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this well, if we don't waste it. I'd keep pushing for workers to get training paid for by the companies making money from AI. Online I'd be fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of that decade. AI work would grow, and I'd be good at it. I'd only worry around 2033 or so, and by then I'd have savings and options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on AI work at Hollow Oak and try to move into a bot-design role elsewhere in a couple of years. I'd save harder and maybe invest a bit in an index fund. I'd keep the hospital idea as a backup and do a first aid course just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, with a small itch at the back of my mind. It's the kind of picture where I come out okay if I'm sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest in an index fund. Have you done that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, but Priya's dad keeps telling us to. I'd start small, maybe fifty a month, and leave it alone. It's not my thing, but ten years is long enough for it to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make ten years feel worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bosses keep all the gains and we just do more chats for the same pay, I'll have less saved by the time AGI hits. That's why the union bit matters even when it's slow.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** if we don't waste it.
I'd push for **company-paid training** funded by AI profits.
think: I'd **do well** for most of the decade as AI work grows.
I'd start worrying around **2033**, with savings and options by then.

S4.quote: If the bosses keep all the gains and we just do more chats for the same pay, I'll have less saved by the time AGI hits.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees AI as **opportunity** first.
She'd try **investing** for the first time, cautiously.
Pay and **fair gains** still matter to her even in the slow picture.

steps.text: Move into a bot-design role at another firm within two years
Keep leading AI work on the Hollow Oak chat team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Being good with AI is my whole plan, and in that one it doesn't matter. What would help is paid time to retrain into hospital work, and a basic income for the gap, because the gap is the scary bit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people like me what we're good at, not just what we're scared of. I've made my team faster with AI and nobody's ever asked me how. If bosses asked agents first, the change might go better for everyone.

headlineQuote: I've made my team faster with AI and nobody's ever asked me how.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** chat agent at Hollow Oak Home, an online furniture shop.
She uses AI **every day** and built saved prompts that the whole team uses.
She shares a flat with **Priya**, a nurse, and has about **five months** saved.
She sees **opportunity** in the slower pictures and plans a move into hospital work for fast AGI.
She wants workers to **share the gains** and would start a union if she had to.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her plan of being good with AI stops mattering.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid time** to retrain into hospital work.
A **basic income** to cover the gap between jobs.
